age.peak: bimodal: young children (scalds) and working-age adults (flames, chemicals, electricity)

demographics: Scalds from hot liquids and steam are the most common burn in young children
Flame and chemical burns are more common in working-age adults, often occupational
Older adults have higher morbidity and mortality for the same burn size
Low socioeconomic status and lack of working smoke detectors are associated with more severe residential fire burns

risk_factors.text: Young child in the home (scalds from hot liquids, steam, bath water)
Occupational exposure to flames, hot surfaces, chemicals or electricity
Smoking and alcohol or substance use
Older adult with impaired mobility, sensation or cognition
Seizure disorder, syncope or neuropathy that impairs escape from a heat source
Impaired judgment or supervision (young children, cognitive impairment)

comorbidities: Coronary artery disease or heart failure
Psychiatric illness including dementia and substance use disorders
social_history: Cooking, bathing or heating with open flame or hot water
Occupational or hobby exposure to fire, hot liquids, chemicals or electricity
Injury pattern inconsistent with the reported mechanism raises concern for abuse or neglect
exposures: Open flame, building fire or flammable liquids and gases

chief_complaints.text: My skin is red and hurts
I have blisters where I got burned

hpi.onset: Sudden, at the moment of contact with the heat source, chemical, electricity or radiation
hpi.duration: Minutes to hours since injury at presentation; deeper burns may evolve over the first 24–48 hours
hpi.progression: Pain and redness are immediate; blisters form over minutes to hours; partial-thickness burns can deepen over the first day or two, especially if cooled poorly or infected
hpi.location: Depends on mechanism: hands, forearms, face and chest with flame; trunk, buttocks, perineum or extremities with scald; mouth and throat with caustic ingestion; often a patterned area matching the source
hpi.radiation: Usually none; pain is localized to the injured skin
hpi.quality: Burning, stinging or throbbing pain; deep full-thickness burns may be numb or painless
hpi.severity: Mild to severe; superficial burns are 2–4/10, partial-thickness burns often 7–10/10, full-thickness burns may be painless
hpi.timing: Constant, worse with air movement, dressing changes and cleaning
relieving: Cool running water applied soon after injury
Acetaminophen or an opioid for pain

associated_symptoms.text: Redness and swelling of the burned skin
Pain out of proportion to the visible injury
Hoarse voice, cough or singed nose hairs after smoke or flame exposure
Numbness over the burned area (deep burn)
Dark or decreased urine after a large burn

pertinent_negatives: Rash or skin lesions before the injury
Itching or new medicines before the injury
Blistering in areas not exposed to the heat source
Bleeding or drainage from the burn at the time of injury
Loss of consciousness at the scene (unless electrical or inhalation injury)
Shortness of breath at rest in a patient with only a small skin burn

positives.text: Pale, leathery or waxy skin in deep burns

argues_against: Widespread rash without a heat source
Fever and rash before any burn exposure

positives.text: Soot in the mouth or nose

argues_against: Chronic obstructive lung disease as the cause of breathlessness
Gastrointestinal bleeding as the cause of shock
Stroke or seizure as the primary cause
Deliberate self-inflicted burn without reported intent

atypical.how_it_differs: Scalds are the most common mechanism; children may not localize pain and present with crying, irritability and refusal to use the affected limb. Non-accidental burn patterns (glove-and-stocking, immersion lines, cigarette burns) should be considered.
Present with poor feeding, lethargy and irritability rather than pain complaints; even small burns can cause significant fluid loss and hypothermia.
Thinner skin means deeper burns from the same exposure; impaired mobility or cognition may delay escape, and mortality is higher for the same burn size. Pain may be blunted by neuropathy.
Peripheral neuropathy can blunt pain, and impaired healing and immune function increase the risk of infection and delayed presentation.
missing_classic_features: Pain out of proportion to the injury

atypical.how_it_differs: Maternal hypovolemia and hypoxemia can compromise the fetus; burns are managed with attention to fetal monitoring and maternal resuscitation.
missing_classic_features: Typical pain and fluid shifts without fetal concern

atypical.how_it_differs: Higher risk of rapid wound infection and sepsis; fever may be absent or blunted.

general.mild: Comfortable, alert, no distress; focused on the burned area
general.moderate: In pain, grimacing, but alert and interactive
general.severe: Distressed, tachycardic, cool extremities, anxious or restless
general.critical: Toxic-appearing, pale, diaphoretic, lethargic or obtunded; may have soot around the mouth or singed facial hair

findings.maneuver: Inspect the burn and note color, blistering, capillary refill and sensation
findings.finding: Superficial (first-degree) burns are red, dry and painful without blisters; partial-thickness (second-degree) burns are blistered, moist, red or mottled and very painful; full-thickness (third-degree) burns are white, waxy, leathery or charred, may be painless, and do not blanch

findings.maneuver: Estimate the percentage of total body surface area burned using the rule of nines (or Lund-Browder in children)
findings.finding: Extent of partial- and full-thickness burn expressed as % TBSA; superficial burns are not counted

findings.maneuver: Inspect the mouth, oropharynx and nose; listen to the voice
findings.finding: Soot in the mouth or nose, singed nasal hairs, facial or oral burns, hoarse voice or stridor suggesting inhalation injury

findings.maneuver: Inspect the burned extremity or chest for a full-thickness circumferential pattern
findings.finding: Tight, unyielding eschar that may impair distal perfusion or chest expansion

findings.maneuver: Check capillary refill, radial or pedal pulses, and sensation distal to the burn
findings.finding: Delayed capillary refill, weak or absent pulses, or numbness distal to a circumferential burn

findings.maneuver: Inspect the burn for purulent drainage, spreading erythema, foul odor or eschar separation
findings.finding: Signs of wound infection or sepsis

findings.maneuver: Inspect skin not exposed to the heat source
findings.finding: No rash, blisters or lesions in unburned areas
Clear breath sounds without wheeze or crackles in a patient without inhalation injury

findings.maneuver: Assess orientation and gross motor function
findings.finding: Alert and oriented without focal deficit (unless electrical injury or hypoxia)

labs.caveat: May be normal early from hemoconcentration; a falling hemoglobin suggests blood loss or hemodilution from resuscitation.
Can be falsely elevated early from plasma loss before fluids are given.
A stress leukocytosis is common in the first 24–48 hours and does not by itself mean infection; a rising count after that suggests wound infection or sepsis.
Thrombocytopenia can reflect dilution from massive resuscitation, consumption or early sepsis.
Hyponatremia from fluid shifts and resuscitation; hypernatremia suggests inadequate free water.
Hypokalemia is common with large-volume resuscitation; hyperkalemia raises concern for electrical injury, rhabdomyolysis or renal failure.
Low bicarbonate suggests metabolic acidosis from shock, poor perfusion or inhalation injury.
Rises with dehydration and hypovolemia; a high BUN/creatinine ratio supports volume depletion.
A rise after a large burn suggests acute kidney injury from hypovolemia, myoglobinuria or sepsis.
Stress hyperglycemia is common and worsens outcomes; tight control is avoided because of hypoglycemia risk.
Falls with the systemic inflammatory response and capillary leak; low values worsen fluid resuscitation requirements.
Markedly elevated in electrical burns, crush injury and deep muscle burns; a very high CK with dark urine suggests rhabdomyolysis and myoglobinuric kidney injury.
Elevated lactate indicates hypoperfusion or shock and guides resuscitation; it also rises with inhalation injury and carbon monoxide exposure.
Acidemia from shock, poor perfusion or inhalation injury; measured on arterial blood gas.
Low from tachypnea and pain; a rising PaCO2 with a hoarse voice or stridor suggests upper airway obstruction from inhalation injury.
Falls with inhalation injury, smoke inhalation or carbon monoxide poisoning; a normal PaO2 does not exclude carbon monoxide toxicity.
Pulse oximetry can read falsely normal in carbon monoxide poisoning because it cannot distinguish carboxyhemoglobin from oxyhemoglobin.
Prolonged with severe burns, disseminated intravascular coagulation or liver dysfunction.
Positive blood without red cells on microscopy suggests myoglobinuria from muscle injury, especially in electrical or deep burns.
High specific gravity reflects dehydration and concentrated urine; urine output is the key resuscitation endpoint.
Negative. Required in anyone who could be pregnant before imaging, medications and resuscitation decisions.

findings.finding: Nonspecific ST-T changes from tachycardia, pain and electrolyte shifts
Prolonged QT interval with hypokalemia, hypocalcemia or hypomagnesemia
Widened QRS with severe hyperkalemia from electrical injury or rhabdomyolysis
ST elevation or depression suggesting myocardial injury in electrical burns or in patients with underlying coronary disease
Ventricular fibrillation or asystole in high-voltage electrical injury

imaging.preferred_when: Suspected inhalation injury, smoke exposure or respiratory symptoms

findings.text: Normal in most patients with a skin burn alone
Patchy alveolar or interstitial opacities from inhalation injury or pulmonary edema
Soot in the trachea or main bronchi
Widened mediastinum or pneumothorax after blast or electrical injury

imaging.preferred_when: Suspected inhalation injury with an unclear chest x-ray, or trauma from a blast or fall

findings.text: Ground-glass and consolidative opacities from inhalation injury
Airway wall thickening and mucus plugging
Pneumothorax, rib fractures or pulmonary contusion from associated trauma

imaging.preferred_when: Electrical injury, loss of consciousness, fall or blast injury

findings.text: Normal study in most patients with a skin burn alone
Intracranial hemorrhage or cerebral edema after electrical injury or head trauma

imaging.preferred_when: Fall, blast injury or electrical injury with neck pain or altered mental status

findings.text: Normal cervical spine in most patients
Fracture or dislocation after a fall or blast

imaging.study: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
imaging.preferred_when: Electrical injury, blunt trauma or unexplained shock

findings.text: Normal study in most patients with a skin burn alone
Solid organ injury, bowel injury or free fluid after blunt trauma

imaging.preferred_when: Electrical burn, deep burn over a joint, or suspected associated fracture

findings.text: Normal bone in most thermal burns
Fracture or dislocation after a fall or electrical injury
Soft tissue swelling or foreign material in the wound

imaging.preferred_when: Suspected inhalation injury with worsening oxygenation or unclear airway findings

findings.text: Erythema, edema, soot or ulceration of the airway mucosa
Carbonaceous material and mucus plugging in the tracheobronchial tree

initial.why: Baseline hemoglobin, white count and platelets; guides resuscitation and later detects infection
Electrolytes, renal function and glucose; guides fluid resuscitation and detects acute kidney injury
Assesses oxygenation, ventilation and acid-base status
initial.only_if: suspected inhalation injury, smoke exposure or respiratory distress

initial.why: Detects hypoperfusion and guides resuscitation in large burns
Urine output and myoglobin screen in large or electrical burns
Rules out pregnancy before imaging, medications and resuscitation decisions
Looks for inhalation injury or associated trauma
initial.only_if: suspected inhalation injury, smoke exposure or respiratory symptoms

confirmatory.why: Direct visualization confirms inhalation injury when the diagnosis is uncertain or the airway is worsening
confirmatory.only_if: suspected inhalation injury with unclear findings or worsening oxygenation

supporting.why: Detects muscle injury and rhabdomyolysis in electrical or deep burns
Detects coagulopathy in large burns or suspected disseminated intravascular coagulation
Characterizes inhalation injury and associated trauma when the chest x-ray is unclear
supporting.only_if: suspected inhalation injury with an unclear chest x-ray or trauma

supporting.why: Evaluates for intracranial injury after electrical injury, fall or blast
supporting.only_if: electrical injury, loss of consciousness, fall or blast injury

supporting.why: Evaluates for cervical spine injury after a fall or blast
supporting.only_if: fall, blast injury or electrical injury with neck pain or altered mental status

supporting.test: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
supporting.why: Evaluates for intra-abdominal injury after electrical or blunt trauma
supporting.only_if: electrical injury, blunt trauma or unexplained shock

supporting.why: Evaluates for fracture or foreign body in electrical or deep burns
supporting.only_if: electrical burn, deep burn over a joint, or suspected associated fracture

not_indicated.why: No role in burn assessment unless abdominal pain suggests pancreatitis
Not needed acutely unless diabetes management is relevant
Not routine; reserved for suspected inhalation injury or trauma
not_indicated.only_if: suspected inhalation injury with an unclear chest x-ray or trauma

not_indicated.why: Not routine; reserved for electrical injury, head trauma or altered mental status
not_indicated.only_if: electrical injury, loss of consciousness, fall or blast injury

not_indicated.why: Not routine; reserved for trauma or electrical injury with neck symptoms
not_indicated.only_if: fall, blast injury or electrical injury with neck pain or altered mental status

not_indicated.test: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
not_indicated.why: Not routine; reserved for electrical injury, blunt trauma or unexplained shock
not_indicated.only_if: electrical injury, blunt trauma or unexplained shock

not_indicated.why: Not routine; reserved for electrical or deep burns with suspected fracture
not_indicated.only_if: electrical burn, deep burn over a joint, or suspected associated fracture

decision_points: Assess airway early in any patient with facial burns, soot, hoarse voice or stridor; intubate before edema makes it difficult
Estimate TBSA with the rule of nines in adults and Lund-Browder in children; superficial burns are not counted
Start fluid resuscitation for burns over 20% TBSA in adults and over 10% in children using the Parkland or modified Brooke formula, then titrate to urine output
Pregnancy test before imaging and medications in anyone who could be pregnant
Suspect carbon monoxide or cyanide toxicity with smoke inhalation and a normal pulse oximetry reading
Consider child abuse or neglect when the burn pattern does not match the reported mechanism

differential.name: Cellulitis
differential.why_considered: Red, warm, swollen and tender skin with fever can mimic a partial-thickness burn, especially when the burn history is vague.
differential.trigger: Spreading redness with fever and no clear heat or chemical exposure

history: No heat, chemical or electrical exposure
Gradual onset over days rather than sudden at the moment of injury
Often a break in the skin, insect bite or prior wound
exam: Poorly demarcated spreading erythema without blisters or a burn pattern
Tender, warm skin with lymphangitic streaking
No charred, waxy or leathery areas
imaging: Ultrasound may show subcutaneous edema or abscess
No findings of inhalation injury on chest imaging

differential.name: Toxic epidermal necrolysis
differential.why_considered: Widespread skin sloughing and blistering can look like a large partial-thickness burn.
differential.trigger: Widespread blistering and skin detachment without any heat or chemical exposure

history: Recent new medication such as an anticonvulsant, allopurinol or sulfonamide
Preceding fever, malaise and mucosal pain
No burn mechanism
exam: Positive Nikolsky sign with sheet-like epidermal detachment
Painful erosions of the mouth, eyes or genitals
Targetoid or dusky macules rather than a patterned burn
labs: Often normal or nonspecific; may show leukopenia or elevated liver enzymes
imaging: Not diagnostic; chest imaging only if respiratory involvement is suspected

differential.name: Stevens-Johnson syndrome
differential.why_considered: Mucosal and skin blistering with systemic illness can resemble a burn.
differential.trigger: Mucosal erosions with skin blistering after a new medication

history: New medication in the preceding weeks
Prodromal fever and sore throat
No exposure to heat, chemicals or electricity
exam: Hemorrhagic crusting of the lips and oral mucosa
Detachment of less than 10% of body surface area
labs: Nonspecific; may show elevated liver enzymes or leukopenia

differential.name: Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome
differential.why_considered: Widespread tender erythema with superficial peeling in a child can mimic a scald.
differential.trigger: A young child with diffuse tender erythema and peeling skin without a heat source

history: Recent conjunctivitis, otitis or nasopharyngeal infection
No burn exposure
Irritability and poor feeding
exam: Superficial, easily peeled skin with a positive Nikolsky sign
labs: Leukocytosis; cultures from the primary site may grow Staphylococcus aureus

differential.name: Contact dermatitis
differential.why_considered: Localized redness, swelling and blistering after chemical or plant exposure can look like a chemical burn.

history: Exposure to an allergen or irritant rather than a caustic
Itching rather than burning pain
Onset hours to days after exposure
exam: Erythematous, vesicular rash with sharp borders matching the contact area

differential.name: Frostbite
differential.why_considered: Cold injury causes skin blistering, numbness and discoloration that can resemble a deep burn.

history: Prolonged exposure to cold, wind or wet conditions
No heat, chemical or electrical exposure
exam: Affected areas are cold, pale or waxy and numb
Distal extremities, nose or ears most affected
imaging: Bone scan or angiography may show absent perfusion in severe cases

differential.name: Necrotizing fasciitis
differential.why_considered: Severe pain, skin discoloration and systemic toxicity can mimic a deep burn with sepsis.
differential.trigger: Pain out of proportion to skin findings with rapid progression and systemic toxicity

history: Often follows a minor wound, surgery or varicella
Rapidly worsening pain over hours
No burn mechanism
exam: Pain out of proportion to visible skin changes
Dusky or bullous skin with crepitus
labs: Marked leukocytosis, elevated lactate and creatinine, hyponatremia
imaging: CT or MRI shows fascial thickening, gas or fluid tracking along fascia

severity.mild: Superficial or small partial-thickness burn, less than 10% TBSA in adults, no airway or inhalation concern, hemodynamically stable, pain controlled with oral analgesia
severity.moderate: Partial-thickness burn of 10–20% TBSA in adults, or any burn with significant pain, blisters or concern for deeper injury, but no airway compromise or shock
severity.severe: Partial- or full-thickness burn over 20% TBSA in adults, or any full-thickness burn, circumferential burn, or burn with inhalation injury or hemodynamic instability
severity.critical: Burn with airway compromise, inhalation injury with respiratory failure, shock, or burns over 40% TBSA; may require immediate intubation, aggressive fluid resuscitation and intensive care

red_flags.finding: Hoarse voice, stridor, soot in the mouth or singed nasal hairs
red_flags.meaning: Inhalation injury with impending airway obstruction; intubate before edema makes it impossible
Burn shock from massive fluid shifts; needs immediate IV fluid resuscitation

red_flags.finding: Circumferential full-thickness burn of the chest or extremity
red_flags.meaning: Restrictive eschar can impair ventilation or distal perfusion; may need escharotomy

red_flags.finding: Dark or decreased urine output after a large burn
red_flags.meaning: Hypovolemia or myoglobinuria with risk of acute kidney injury

red_flags.finding: Altered mental status or loss of consciousness at the scene
red_flags.meaning: Carbon monoxide poisoning, hypoxia, head trauma or electrical injury

red_flags.finding: Burn pattern inconsistent with the reported mechanism
red_flags.meaning: Concern for abuse or neglect, especially in children and older adults

complications.name: Inhalation injury with airway obstruction or respiratory failure
clues: Facial burns, soot or singed nasal hairs

complications.name: Carbon monoxide or cyanide toxicity
clues: Normal pulse oximetry despite severe hypoxia

complications.name: Wound infection and sepsis
clues: Purulent drainage, foul odor or spreading erythema
Fever, rising white count or hemodynamic instability

complications.name: Acute kidney injury
clues: Dark urine or positive urine blood without red cells

complications.name: Heterotopic ossification
clues: Decreased range of motion months after injury

special_populations.differences: Scalds are the most common mechanism; use the Lund-Browder chart for TBSA because the head is proportionally larger. Fluid resuscitation starts at 10% TBSA rather than 20%. Non-accidental burn patterns should be considered.
Present with poor feeding, lethargy and irritability rather than pain complaints. Even small burns can cause significant fluid loss and hypothermia; maintain warmth during assessment.

Thinner skin means deeper burns from the same exposure; impaired mobility or cognition may delay escape. Mortality is higher for the same burn size, and fluid resuscitation must be balanced against cardiac and renal comorbidity.
Maternal hypovolemia and hypoxemia can compromise the fetus. Resuscitate the mother aggressively with attention to fetal monitoring and left uterine displacement after 20 weeks.

Peripheral neuropathy can blunt pain and delay presentation; impaired healing and immune function increase the risk of wound infection. Glucose control is important but tight control is avoided because of hypoglycemia risk.
Higher risk of rapid wound infection and sepsis; fever may be absent or blunted, so a low threshold for cultures and imaging is needed.

key_questions.question: What caused the burn, and what was the source?
key_questions.looking_for: Scald, flame, hot surface, chemical, electrical, radiation or smoke; guides depth, workup and disposition

key_questions.question: When did the burn happen?
key_questions.looking_for: Minutes to hours ago; partial-thickness burns can deepen over the first 24–48 hours

key_questions.question: Was the burn cooled with running water, and was anything applied to it?
key_questions.looking_for: Early cool running water limits depth; butter, toothpaste or ice worsen injury

key_questions.question: Where on the body is the burn, and how much of the body does it cover?
key_questions.looking_for: Face, hands, feet, perineum, circumferential or large areas change disposition and fluid needs

key_questions.question: Did the burn happen in an enclosed space, or was there smoke, soot or hot gas?
key_questions.looking_for: Inhalation injury, carbon monoxide or cyanide exposure

key_questions.question: Is your voice hoarse, or do you have a cough, trouble breathing or throat tightness?
key_questions.looking_for: Airway edema from inhalation injury; intubate before obstruction

key_questions.question: Did you lose consciousness at the scene or fall?
key_questions.looking_for: Electrical injury, carbon monoxide poisoning, head or spine trauma

key_questions.question: How bad is the pain, and is any part of the burn numb?
key_questions.looking_for: Numbness suggests full-thickness burn; pain out of proportion suggests deeper injury

key_questions.question: Are you able to drink and keep fluids down?
key_questions.looking_for: Oral intake determines whether IV fluids are needed for smaller burns

key_questions.question: Have you had any fever, chills or worsening redness since the burn?
What medical problems do you have, such as diabetes, heart disease or nerve damage?
key_questions.looking_for: Comorbidities that worsen healing, blunt pain or complicate fluid resuscitation

key_questions.question: What medicines do you take?
key_questions.looking_for: Beta blockers or opioids that blunt tachycardia, and drugs affecting healing

key_questions.question: Do you have any medication allergies?
key_questions.looking_for: Allergy to sulfa drugs, which affects topical antibiotic choice

key_questions.question: Could you be pregnant? When was your last period?
key_questions.looking_for: Pregnancy changes imaging, medications and resuscitation decisions

key_questions.question: How did the burn happen exactly — could it have been caused by someone else or by a lack of supervision?
key_questions.looking_for: Pattern inconsistent with the mechanism raises concern for abuse or neglect

key_questions.question: Do you have working smoke detectors at home, and do you smoke or use alcohol or drugs?
key_questions.looking_for: Risk factors for more severe burns and impaired escape

reasoning_points: A clear mechanism of heat, chemical, electrical or radiation exposure with sudden onset of pain and skin changes at the moment of injury
Depth assessed from color, blistering, capillary refill and sensation: superficial, partial-thickness or full-thickness
Extent estimated as percent total body surface area using the rule of nines in adults and Lund-Browder in children, counting only partial- and full-thickness burns
Airway and inhalation injury assessed from facial burns, soot, singed nasal hairs, hoarse voice or stridor
Hemodynamic status and urine output used to recognize burn shock and guide fluid resuscitation

Look-alikes such as cellulitis, toxic epidermal necrolysis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome, contact dermatitis, frostbite and necrotizing fasciitis excluded by history, exposure and examination
Pregnancy excluded before imaging, medications and resuscitation decisions
Burn pattern compared with the reported mechanism to screen for abuse or neglect

easy: Clear scald or flame mechanism with a patterned burn
Obvious partial-thickness burn with blisters and severe pain
Small burn under 10% TBSA in a healthy adult
No airway, inhalation or hemodynamic concern
medium: Burn of 10–20% TBSA requiring fluid resuscitation and admission decisions
Mixed-depth burn that is difficult to classify
Facial burn with concern for inhalation injury but a normal chest x-ray
Child with a scald and a mechanism that needs to be verified
hard: Full-thickness burn that is painless and mistaken for a less severe injury
Circumferential chest or extremity burn with impaired ventilation or distal perfusion
Electrical burn with deep muscle injury, rhabdomyolysis and cardiac arrhythmia
Smoke inhalation with carbon monoxide toxicity and falsely normal pulse oximetry
Older adult with a small burn but high mortality and comorbidity limiting resuscitation
Burn pattern inconsistent with the reported mechanism suggesting abuse or neglect
